title: Passover, the freedom meal
hookLine: each year families retell the going out from Egypt around a table (Exodus 12)

cards: A long table, extra chairs borrowed from the neighbors. A plate in the middle with odd things on it: a bone, a roasted egg, bitter herbs, a paste of apples and nuts. Crackers that look like they've been ironed flat.
The youngest child at the table stands up, a little nervous, and asks the question everyone has been waiting for: why is this night different from all other nights?
The grown-ups answer with an ancient story, told as if it happened to them. Today: Pesach, Passover.

teach.b: Exodus tells the story. The Israelites are slaves in Egypt. Moses asks Pharaoh to let them go, plagues fall, and on the last night God passes over the houses of the Israelites, marked with the blood of a lamb.
Pesach comes from that verb: to pass over.

teach.h: NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.
teach.b: They leave in such a hurry the bread has no time to rise, which is why the flat bread, matzah, is eaten for the whole festival. Then the Torah does something unusual: it commands the retelling.
In the King James words: "And thou shalt shew thy son in that day, saying, This is done because of that which the LORD did unto me when I came forth out of Egypt." Unto me, not unto my ancestors.

teach.h: AS IF YOU WENT OUT YOURSELF.
teach.b: The Mishnah takes that seriously: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally went out of Egypt. So the Seder, the ordered meal, is built to make you taste it.

teach.h: BITTER HERBS, SALT WATER, FOUR CUPS.
teach.b: Bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery. Salt water for tears. Four cups of wine for freedom.
The book at the table, the Haggadah, answers the child's question with today's line: we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and now we are free. Look back at the week. Shema, hear.
Brit, a promise kept. Torah, learned together. Tikkun olam, repair.
Bracha, blessed is. Shabbat, rest arrives. And Pesach: a people who remember freedom by eating it, together, every year.

how: Each spring Jewish families hold a Seder on the first night of Passover (the first two nights in many communities outside Israel), reading the Haggadah, eating matzah and bitter herbs, and answering the children's questions.

games.why: the Haggadah answers with the story, told in the first person, and the food on the table makes it tasted.

practice: Remember one story of freedom: a family story of someone who crossed a border, left a bad job, got sober, walked out of something, or your own. Tell it to yourself the Passover way, as if it happened to you, in the present tense.
Notice what was bitter, and what was sweet.

wordCard.voice: Pesach. Passover: the festival that retells the going out from Egypt around a table, so each generation tastes freedom. Today's word.
